pr_title: udev: Fix unit restarts from udev unavailability during systemd upgrade
pr_body:
During systemd 255 -> 256 live upgrade, some users see all units associated with the default target restart. This seems to be triggered by all udev devices going to plugged -> dead state, triggering all mount units to stop and all downstream units to do the same. This is due to temporary udev unavailability from the upgrade.

While we're still root causing this, to be more robust to udev unavailability, we move the unit into DEVICE_TENTATIVE state if its seen by the kernel but not udev on manager startup. Then udev will move it into correct state upon coming up.

Note: I'm not convinced this is the right fix and we need to test this internally to see if it will solve the issue. I'm putting this up to get a sense of if this is viable or way off track.

Fixes: #35329
pr_comments:
@poettering you might have comments on this PR since state checks used to work this way and then it was changed in your commit: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/commit/f62009410a72f5a89bfb8fdd7e48d9d472a6887b

> This reworks how we enter tentative state and does so only when a device was previously not announced via udev. The previous check actually just checked whether a new state bit was set, which is not correct.
And this commit is about pid1, not udev.

Based on @YHNdnzj feedback, I don't think this is the right fix. I am trying another fix to not set state if device is currently being processed by udev (+ adding some debug logging). I will try out fix internally, then post once I have some results.

issue_context.title: systemd daemon-reexec brings down device units if processing by udev (ID_PROCESSING=1)
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

256

### Used distribution

Centos 9

### Linux kernel version used

6.4

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd, systemd-udevd

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

## Background

At Meta, we have seen the following while upgrading systemd 255 -> 256 on a live Centos 9 system during our host provisioning process:
1. We have a service chef-firstboot-os.service that runs Chef and does the RPM upgrade.
3. Right after daemon-reexec and udevd restart (triggered by 255 -> 256 RPM specs), we see Chef receives a SIGTERM from systemd
4. Chef then is SIGKILLed 30s later due to TimeoutStopSec=30s for the unit

This occurs about 5-10% of the time and unfortunately I don't have a reliable local repro after a month - I can only reproduce on the host provisioning systems. The best I have is logs from PID1/udevd/Chef/bpftrace which I'm happy to share.

## Details

While upgrading systemd RPMs from 255 -> 256 under a single DNF transaction, we see Chef gets sent SIGTERM:

## TL;DR - Current theory

When PID1 reloads/reexecs, it calls manager_enumerate() to enumerate the devices in sysfs via device_enumerate(): https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/5b2926d9414f4333153ebe0bf169e1dd76129119/src/core/manager.c#L1853

However, if udev is reloading during the time, the manager may not find any devices registered in udev.

Then the manager will transition the devices from plugged -> dead, even if the mount is found in /proc/self/mountinfo: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/5b2926d9414f4333153ebe0bf169e1dd76129119/src/core/device.c#L195

Since many of our mount units have implicit dependency on these devices (see systemd.mount man page), the mount units are stopped. And because the mount units are stopped, all units associated with the default target (e.g. chef-firstboot-os) are stopped. Once udev comes back up, the devices come back and all units are restarted. But since chef-firstboot-os is a oneshot service, its not restarted.

## Possible solutions

1. Don't do the restart of systemd-udevd and manager reload/reexec at the same time. Basically, we can take restarting udevd out of the RPM spec and restart it in Chef after the RPM upgrade is complete. While it doesn't fix the issue, it reduces the likelihood of a race here. This also may be good as its pretty rare to do systemd major version live upgrades like Meta does.
2. If the device is found in /proc/self/mountinfo but not udev, move it into DEVICE_TENTATIVE state, regardless of if it was previously seen by udev or not. Udev will eventually load and correct it. I put up a PR for this since its straightforward (but looking for feedback in case it has side effects): https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35330
3. If many devices transition to dead on manager reload/reexec, udev may have been down. So ping udev waiting for it to be up, then enumerate the devices again. However, this adds a manager -> udevd RPC dependency which we may not want for distros that don't use udevd.

## Open questions I need to answer
1. Why do devices not show up in sysfs while udev is reloading during 255 -> 256 upgrade? Need to add debug logs to get this info.
2. Why does PID1 restart all targets and units associated with default target (e.g. chef-firstboot-os) instead of just the mounts? We don't use BindTo= or StopPropagatedFrom=
3. Why does this only happen on 255 -> 256 upgrade and not 255 -> 255? We did several of the latter upgrades with no issues.

@yuwata heh you read my mind :) I was looking at that commit. I have a patch that skips setting state in device_catchup() if a device was being processed by udev in device_enumerate(). I'm testing it internally now to see if it fixes the issue and if it works, I'll send it upstream.

EDIT: This is the patch we're testing internally: https://git.centos.org/rpms/systemd/pull-request/23#

@ryantimwilson Nice! Sorry, I did not notice your comment, and pushed #35332.

There are good and bad news.
Good: The issue is reproduced and fixed by the PR.
Bad: The issue can be triggered so easily!! Ugh...

@ryantimwilson So, you are trying to make PID1 handle ID_PROCESSING=1 property correctly. But, let's revert the commit at first like #35332, as we have already released -rc2, and I do not want to change anything large, especially for such very very core part of systemd.

I think PID1 actually should correctly handle the flag, but let's do that after v257-final is released. Of course, patch is welcome. Thank you for working on the issue. And sorry about introducing such terrible issue ;-p
@yuwata we verified PR https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/35332 fixes the issue internally, thanks again! Feel free to close the issue once the PR is merged

review_comments:
Hmm? Is this really the right fix? First of all, I doubt restarting services before reexec-ing pid1 is ever a correct practice here. And secondly, sd-device uses udev db, which sticks around during normal udevd restarts.

The only case where udev db is gone and we need such "downgrade" treatment is during switch-root, and that's handled specifically in device_coldplug(). At the very minimum this change shall also be confined to certain degree. It's not applicable to the generic device_found_changed() func...

> Hmm? Is this really the right fix? First of all, I doubt restarting services before reexec-ing pid1 is ever a correct practice here.

So in our case, we restart udev after reexec/reload. But it still seems to be triggering this...still debugging this.

> And secondly, sd-device uses udev db, which sticks around during normal udevd restarts.

Interesting...maybe there's a udev db incompatibility between 255 and 256 and thus udev needs to regenerate the whole DB, bringing the devices down...I can explore this

> The only case where udev db is gone and we need such "downgrade" treatment is during switch-root, and that's handled specifically in device_coldplug(). At the very minimum this change shall also be confined to certain degree. It's not applicable to the generic device_found_changed() func...

Fair, let me try to confine it further, it really only needs to happen during device_catchup()

@YHNdnzj would you recommend another approach? I know https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/35329 is a long read, but any pointers or debugging tips you might have would be great!
